lessons.lesson: EdgeDesk named Ole Miss as better in market and the game went the other way, across 2 separate published claims. One game does not overturn a season-long rating, but this is the direction to watch: the result landed on the market’s side of the disagreement

lessons.pregame_expectation: 8 of the claims in this article rested on model, passing, rushing, matchup.
lessons.actual_result: None of them could be graded: no single-game statistic in EdgeDesk’s vocabulary observes this driver; the read does not name a side, so there is no direction to test.
lessons.lesson: EdgeDesk prices these games partly on signals it has no way to observe afterwards. That is not an error in the model — it is a gap in the audit, and it means the platform cannot tell, from results alone, whether those parts of the number are earning their weight.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Consider whether a postgame data source exists for model, passing, rushing.

lessons.actual_result: It graded a win. The reasoning behind it did not hold: 1 of 1 gradeable claims went the other way. The read of this matchup was wrong in its mechanism, not only in its number.
lessons.lesson: A winning number built on a reading the game contradicted. Nothing about this result should increase confidence in the mechanism EdgeDesk named, and treating it as confirmation is how a model gets worse while its record gets better.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Why did the number land while the mechanism failed? Either the number was right for a reason EdgeDesk has not identified, or it was luck. Both are worth knowing and they are different.

lessons.lesson: The market had the better estimate here. EdgeDesk’s disagreement was not information on this game, and the honest reading is that the price already contained what the model thought it had found.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Track disagreements of this size across the season. The question is not whether one landed; it is whether the class of them has any edge at all.
